title: Schweikert SMARTER Act Would Replace H-1B Lottery With Merit Points System
excerpt: Arizona Republican's H.R. 10460 would scrap the lottery, set an initial 85,000 cap under a new board, and remove per-country green card caps — but it remains in committee, not law.
body:
• Rep. David Schweikert (R-Ariz.) has introduced the SMARTER Act, H.R. 10460, to replace the H-1B lottery with a merit-based, points-driven selection system starting from an initial cap of 85,000 visas.
  • The bill would remove per-country caps on employment-based immigration — a change that could affect Indian professionals who face decades-long green card waits — but relief would depend on the final visa limits set by a new five-member board.
  • Family sponsorship would be narrowed mainly to spouses and minor children and the Diversity Visa lottery would end; the bill is in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing scheduled and is not law.
  • For Indian applicants today, nothing changes yet: current H-1B registration, lottery and green card rules still apply unless Congress passes the bill.

Washington — A Republican lawmaker has proposed replacing the H-1B visa lottery with a merit-based system that would rank skilled workers by qualifications, salary and economic contribution, in a sweeping employment-immigration overhaul.

The Securing Migration, Addressing Reform, and Talent Enhancement and Retention (SMARTER) Act was introduced by Rep. David Schweikert of Arizona, chairman of the Joint Economic Committee. The bill was introduced on September 16 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, according to reporting based on IANS inputs. The Joint Economic Committee announced the legislation on October 19, linking it to a March 18 hearing on labor inflows and competitiveness and to an issue brief titled “Young, Talented, and Ready: Pivoting Toward a National Scheme of Points-Based Immigration.”

How the merit system would work

Under the proposal, the current lottery-based H-1B selection process would be scrapped. An initial annual limit of 85,000 visas — mirroring the current H-1B ceiling — would apply under the revised skilled-worker framework, with future allocations set by a new five-member Skilled Migration and Recruitment of Talent Board.

https://x.com/lalitkjha/status/2112583667910689052

The board would assess labor shortages, unemployment, wages, productivity and economic conditions to determine allocations across industries. For employment-based permanent residency, a points-based system would consider age, education, English proficiency, earnings and professional achievements. Reporting on the bill says applicants aged 26 to 30 would receive the highest age-related scores, while higher qualifications and salaries significantly above the median household income in an applicant’s state would add points.

Schweikert framed the bill as a response to an aging population and federal debt. The Joint Economic Committee said Republican staff estimate the act would save the federal government approximately $335 billion and increase U.S. GDP by at least $549 billion over 10 years. Those are projections from the bill’s proponents and have not been independently established.

"If we are serious about tackling our debt, growing our economy, and safeguarding our earned federal benefits, we must cultivate a workforce that continues to compete globally at the highest level."

— Rep. David Schweikert, Chairman, Joint Economic Committee

Read the committee’s announcement on the Joint Economic Committee website and the bill listing for H.R. 10460 on Congress.gov.

What it would mean for Indian professionals

Indian nationals receive the largest share of H-1B visas and face the longest employment-based green card backlogs because per-country limits restrict any one country to a small share of visas each year, regardless of demand. The SMARTER Act would remove country-specific caps on employment-based immigration.

That change, on its own, would not guarantee shorter waits. As the reporting notes, the actual impact would depend on the overall limits the new board sets and how the points system allocates visas. The bill also includes transitional provisions for certain pending applications and would give some long-delayed employment-based applicants greater flexibility to change employers — a practical issue for Indian professionals who can wait years in the queue.

At the same time, other parts of the bill would narrow other pathways. Family-sponsored immigration would be restricted mainly to spouses and minor children, eliminating several existing family-preference categories. The Diversity Visa Programme, which allocates up to 55,000 visas a year by lottery to nationals of countries with historically lower immigration, would be ended entirely. The bill would also introduce a gold-card programme for eligible applicants making substantial financial payments and direct the Department of Homeland Security to use artificial intelligence to identify visa overstays.

What happens next

The bill has not become law. It sits in the House Judiciary Committee without a scheduled hearing, in a Congress where comprehensive immigration legislation has repeatedly stalled. Earlier Joint Economic Committee work had already called for replacing the H-1B lottery structure with a merit-based system limited to applicants expected to provide the greatest economic value.

Employers and Indian H-1B holders should plan under current rules while watching the committee process. If the SMARTER Act advances, the details that will matter most are the board’s visa numbers, the final points formula, and how pending green card cases are treated in transition.
